trap.wrong: "Check stock, then decrement it" (or "cache the stock count in Redis and decrement it").
trap.why: Check-then-act races oversell under concurrency, and a cache-only counter can lose decrements on failover or drift from the database.
trap.probe: Atomic reservation, a single source of truth for stock, reservation expiry, and protecting the system from the spike.
trap.say: "Stock is decremented atomically with a conditional update or token-based reservation, reservations expire if unpaid, and a queue or waiting room in front keeps the spike from overwhelming the database."

thesis: Overselling is a concurrency bug; the spike is a load problem. Solve the first with atomic reservations against a single source of truth with expiring holds, and the second with admission control, a waiting room, and moving the hot counter off the main database path.
pitch: Correctness first: the decrement must be atomic, for example UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE sku = :sku AND available > 0, checking the affected rows, or pre-generating 1,000 reservation tokens and letting each buyer claim one atomically. A successful claim creates a time-limited hold; if payment doesn't complete in, say, 10 minutes, the hold expires and the unit returns to stock. Load second: 500,000 people hitting one row will serialise on that row and overload everything around it. So I'd put a waiting room or queue in front to admit buyers at a rate the system handles, shard the counter into buckets (for example 10 buckets of 100 units) or keep the counter in an atomic in-memory store with durable logging, and serve the product page from cache. Orders are confirmed only when payment completes, and a reconciliation job checks holds, orders and stock agree.

points.d: A conditional update on the stock row, or claiming one of N pre-created tokens, so two buyers can never take the same unit.
Reserve on 'buy', confirm on payment, release on timeout. Without expiry, abandoned carts lock stock forever.
One authoritative stock record or token pool. Caches may display availability but never decide it.
Admit users at a controlled rate, give them a queue position, and reject or defer the rest gracefully.
Split stock across N buckets so updates spread across rows or keys; a buyer tries a random bucket, then others.
Cache the product page, isolate the sale path from regular traffic, and rate-limit per user and per device.
Compare holds, orders and stock after the sale to catch bugs, and fix with clear customer communication.

decision: Atomic reservation with expiring holds for correctness, always. Add waiting rooms and counter sharding as scale requires. Deliberate overselling (with compensation) is a business decision, not an accident.
numbers: A single hot row taking 2 ms per update serialises to about 500 updates per second; 10 buckets raise the ceiling to roughly 5,000 per second.
1,000 units with a 10-minute payment hold: if 30% abandon, those units return to stock within 10 minutes.
pitfalls: Redis-only counters with no durable record or reconciliation.
Letting the spike hit the main database and taking down unrelated features.

followups.q: How do you make the waiting room fair?
followups.a: Randomise positions among users who arrived before the start, then serve in order; tie queue tokens to verified accounts to stop bots.

followups.q: What if payment succeeds just after the hold expired and the unit was resold?
followups.a: Detect it at confirmation (hold no longer valid), refund automatically, and notify the customer; keep a small buffer if the business prefers to honour such orders.
Per-account and per-device limits, bot detection, verified accounts for the sale, and purchase limits per customer.

example: A sneaker drop pre-created 2,000 reservation tokens in a sharded table. A waiting room admitted 3,000 users per minute; each claimed a token atomically and had 8 minutes to pay. The sale sold out in 14 minutes with zero oversells, and unpaid holds returned 240 units to the pool.
